claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel contains inherent MnS inclusions.
Sulfide inclusions in untreated Q235 steel are primarily MnS.
MnS inclusions act as localized cathodic sites relative to the ferritic matrix.
Micro-galvanic coupling to MnS creates anodic regions in the surrounding iron matrix.
The MnS-associated micro-galvanic cells accelerate dissolution of the surrounding iron matrix.
Chloride penetration enhances MnS-associated localized corrosion.
Elevated temperature accelerates the proposed corrosion mechanism through increased ionic mobility and reaction rates.
Selective acid pickling or precision polishing can remove or passivate MnS inclusions while leaving the bulk Q235 steel mostly unaltered.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution is an applicable corrosion-test environment for Q235-based specimens.
Removing or passivating MnS inclusions will delay pitting initiation relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Removing or passivating MnS inclusions will reduce corrosion-related weight loss relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Removing or passivating MnS inclusions will produce more stable open-circuit potentials than those of untreated Q235 steel.
The protective effect of MnS removal or passivation will occur at both approximately 25°C and 70°C.
The difference in corrosion behavior between treated and untreated samples will be more pronounced at 70°C than at 25°C.
Untreated, as-received Q235 steel typically exhibits localized pitting and accelerated degradation in aggressive chloride-containing conditions.
The proposed mechanism is limited to Q235 steel having a typical inclusion and minor-impurity profile.
The proposed mechanism may not govern when uniform corrosion dominates.
Grain-boundary condition and residual stress may also contribute to corrosion behavior.
A null improvement in treated specimens is proposed as falsification of MnS inclusions being the primary driver of localized corrosion.
